questions.question:
Consider the following array.

[latex]\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline 23&32&45&69&72&73&89&97 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Which algorithm out of the following options uses the least number of comparisons (among the array elements) to sort the above array in ascending order?

options.D: Quicksort using the last element as pivot

questions.explanation:
The array is already sorted.
- Insertion sort: each element is compared once with its left neighbour [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] n [latex]-[/latex] 1 = 7 comparisons (best case).
- Selection sort always does n(n [latex]-[/latex] 1)/2 = 28.
- Merge sort needs more than 7 (about 12 here).
- Quicksort with the last element as pivot on sorted input is the worst case (28).

Answer: Insertion sort

questions.question:
Let G be a connected undirected weighted graph. Consider the following two statements.

S1: There exists a minimum weight edge in G which is present in every minimum spanning tree of G.
S2: If every edge in G has distinct weight, then G has a unique minimum spanning tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: Both S1 and S2 are true
options.B: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.C: S1 is false and S2 is true
options.D: Both S1 and S2 are false

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: if several edges share the minimum weight (e.g. a triangle with all weights 1), each MST leaves out one of them, so no single minimum edge is in every MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- S2: distinct weights [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] unique MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: S1 is false and S2 is true

questions.question:
Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] as input.

[latex]\texttt{someAlgo(G)}:[/latex]
1. Let [latex]v[/latex] be any vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] starting at [latex]v[/latex]. Let [latex]u[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex] at maximum distance from [latex]v[/latex] as given by the BFS.
2. Run BFS on [latex]G[/latex] again with [latex]u[/latex] as the starting vertex. Let [latex]z[/latex] be the vertex at maximum distance from [latex]u[/latex] as given by the BFS.
3. Output the distance between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]z[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex].

The output of [latex]\texttt{someAlgo(T)}[/latex] for the tree shown in the given figure is __________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
This is the standard double-BFS algorithm for computing a tree's diameter (the longest path between any two nodes): BFS from an arbitrary vertex [latex]v[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex], then BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] to find the farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex] — the distance from [latex]u[/latex] to [latex]z[/latex] is guaranteed to equal the tree's true diameter (a classical, provable property specific to trees: whichever vertex is farthest from an arbitrary start must be one endpoint of some longest path).

Looking at the given tree: it has a central hub vertex from which several branches radiate outward — one branch (upper-left) extends out through a couple of intermediate vertices before forking further, another shorter branch goes off to the lower-left, and a branch on the right extends out and forks again near its far end. The two "longest reaching" branches from the hub are the upper-left branch and the right-hand branch.

Running BFS from any starting vertex [latex]v[/latex] will find some farthest vertex [latex]u[/latex] (this will land at the tip of one of the long branches, e.g. the far end of the upper-left branch). Running BFS again from [latex]u[/latex] then reaches all the way across the hub to the tip of the opposite long branch (the far end of the right-hand branch) as the new farthest vertex [latex]z[/latex]. Counting edges along this path — from the upper-left branch tip, back through its intermediate vertices, through the hub, and back out through the right-hand branch to its tip — gives a total of [latex]6[/latex] edges, matching the tree's actual diameter.

Answer: 6

questions.question: Let G = (V, E) be a simple undirected graph, and s be a particular vertex in it called the source. For [latex]x \in V[/latex], let d(x) denote the shortest distance in G from s to x. A breadth first search (BFS) is performed starting at s. Let T be the resultant BFS tree. If (u,v) is an edge of G that is not in T, then which one of the following CANNOT be the value of d(u)-d(v)?
questions.explanation:
In BFS of an undirected graph, every edge joins vertices whose levels differ by at most 1. If d(u) [latex]-[/latex] d(v) were 2, v would have discovered u earlier, giving d(u) = d(v) + 1.

So d(u) [latex]-[/latex] d(v) can only be [latex]-[/latex]1, 0 or 1.

Answer: 2

questions.question:
Let G be a weighted graph with edge weights greater than one and G' be the graph constructed by
squaring the weights of edges in G. Let T and T' be the minimum spanning trees of G and G',
respectively, with total weights t and t'. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: T' = T with total weight  [latex]t' = t^{2}[/latex]
options.B: T' = T with total weight  [latex]t' \lt  t^{2}[/latex]
options.C: T' [latex]\neq[/latex] T but total weight  [latex]t' = t^{2}[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Squaring weights greater than 1 keeps their order, so the same tree stays minimum. But the total weight is [latex]t'=\sum w_i^2[/latex], not [latex]t^2=(\sum w_i)^2[/latex].

- [latex]t'=t^2[/latex] is false in general.
- [latex]t'\lt t^2[/latex] fails when the tree has a single edge ([latex]t'=t^2[/latex]).
- With equal weights there can be several MSTs, so T' need not be the same T.

None of the options is always true.

Answer: None of the above

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
questions.explanation:
For a directed acyclic graph (DAG), the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary).

This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the condition given below.

[latex]\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}[/latex] such that [latex]i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])[/latex]

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
questions.explanation:
The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex").

This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds.

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]

questions.question:
Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be a directed, weighed graph with weight function [latex]w:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex]. For some function [latex]f:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex], for each edge [latex](u,v) \in E[/latex], define [latex]w'(u,v)[/latex] as [latex]w(u,v)+f(u)-f(v)[/latex].

Which one of the options completes the following sentence so that it is TRUE?

"The shortest paths in G under [latex]w[/latex] are shortest paths under [latex]w'[/latex] too,_________".

options.B: if and only if [latex]\forall u \in V,f(u)[/latex] is positive
options.C: if and only if [latex]\forall u \in V,f(u)[/latex] is negative
options.D: if and only if f(u) is the distance from s to u in the graph obtained by adding a new vertex s to G and edges of zero weight from s to every verex of G

questions.explanation:
For any path [latex]s=v_0\rightarrow v_1\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow v_k=t[/latex], the f-terms cancel in pairs:
[latex]w'(\text{path})=w(\text{path})+f(s)-f(t)[/latex]

Every s-to-t path changes by the same constant [latex]f(s)-f(t)[/latex], so the shortest one stays shortest, for any f. (This is the reweighting trick in Johnson's algorithm.)

Answer: for every [latex]f:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of [latex]G[/latex] is/are true?

options.A: In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the largest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is not in any MST
options.B: In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is in every MST
options.C: For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the largest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is not in any MST
options.D: For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is in every MST

questions.explanation:
When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique, and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply:

- Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True.
- The claim about the smallest-weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping).
- The claim that the largest-weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph.
- Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True.

Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST.
